name: Hobble skirt

card.summary: A narrow-hemmed early-1900s skirt that gave women a long, slim, tapered column silhouette from hip to ankle.
card.note: The narrow hem sharply shortens stride and was linked to falls and boarding difficulty in period reports.

quick.overview:
The hobble skirt was a women's skirt that narrowed toward the ankle, creating an unbroken, slender vertical line from waist to hem. Popular roughly between 1908 and 1914, it was associated with the couturier Paul Poiret, and it is remembered as one of fashion's clearest examples of a silhouette that changes how the legs and whole figure look.

Its visual payoff was a long, streamlined, column-like body shape. The price was mobility: the tight hem forced short steps, and newspapers, cartoonists and some physicians commented on the restriction. Designers answered with slits, hidden pleats and ties.
quick.how: Wearers chose a fitted skirt in silk, wool or similar fabric that followed the hips and thighs and narrowed at or near the ankle. Period adaptations included slit or wrap versions and hidden pleats that allowed a little more stride, and some women reportedly wore a tie or fetter to keep the hem from splitting. Modern designers have periodically revived narrow-hem pencil and sheath shapes.
quick.risks: Contemporary reports linked the style to falls, difficulty boarding streetcars and several deaths, and some doctors of the time criticised it for restricting leg movement. Cities adapted transit (for example step-free streetcars in New York in 1912). The narrow cut also limited walking speed, so period commentary often described a 'mincing' gait.

lead: The hobble skirt was a women's skirt with a narrow hem that significantly restricted the wearer's stride, a short-lived fashion that peaked between about 1908 and 1914; the name comes from the way it 'hobbled' the person walking in it. [1] People wore it to get a long, slim, tapering line from hip to ankle, a more columnar shape than the full, bell-shaped skirts and S-curve silhouette that came before. [1][2]

The couturier Paul Poiret claimed credit for the style, although it is unclear whether he actually invented it. [1] Wikipedia's account notes that skirts had already been narrowing since the mid-1900s, and that slim cuts also used less fabric. [1] Poiret is also credited with abandoning the corset in his house in 1906, and he is reported to have said that he freed the bust but shackled the legs. [3]

Because it limited walking, the skirt was widely satirised in cartoons and postcards and was blamed in newspaper accounts for falls and accidents. It faded as World War I began, but narrow-hem silhouettes returned repeatedly in later decades. [1]

angle.text: Wearers used the hobble skirt to present a slim, tubular, elongated figure instead of the full-skirted Edwardian shape. The look came from the cut of the garment itself, at the cost of a much shorter stride.

paras: The hobble skirt fitted closely over the hips and thighs and tapered to a narrow hem at or near the ankle, producing a columnar silhouette. [1][2] Fabrics described in period fashion included silk, wool and taffeta, often draped or cut to follow the body. [2]
Skirts had been getting narrower since the mid-1900s, and the slim cut also saved fabric. [1] The style replaced the padded, S-curved shape of the early Edwardian period with a straighter line. [2]

One story ties the style to a 1908 demonstration by the Wright brothers in Le Mans, France, where Edith Ogilby Berg became the first American woman to fly as a passenger; she tied her skirt at the ankles to keep it from blowing about, and a French designer is said to have drawn on the image. [1] Poiret may have been that designer, and he claimed the hobble skirt as his own. [1]
Poiret's house was among the most visible in Paris, and his designs, shown in Paris and reported in New York, helped spread the shape among fashionable women in urban centres. [2][3]

The narrow hem made boarding streetcars difficult; New York ran hobble-skirt cars with no step up in 1912, and Los Angeles introduced similar cars in 1913. [1] Some wearers fastened a fetter or tied their knees together so the skirt would not split. [1]

Designers adapted: Jeanne Paquin hid pleats in her skirts, and Lucile offered slit or wrap versions. [1] Wikipedia lists several deaths linked to the skirt in newspaper accounts, including a 1910 death at a Paris racetrack and the 1911 drowning of an eighteen-year-old after a fall from an Erie Canal bridge. [1] Grokipedia describes physicians of the 1910s criticising the style for restricting leg movement and exercise. [2]

The skirt inspired hundreds of cartoons and comic postcards, one series calling it the 'speed-limit skirt', and some women reportedly raced in them as a joke. [1] Commentators have read it both as a step away from corsetry and as a new form of constraint. [2][3]

The trend faded at the start of World War I, when restricted mobility suited wartime life poorly. [1] Narrow skirts returned with Christian Dior's sheath skirts in 1948, Pierre Cardin, Simonetta and Yves Saint Laurent around 1957-1960 (Saint Laurent's Fall 1959 collection was nicknamed his 'hobble skirt' collection), Cardin again in 1970, and figure-hugging stretch sheaths from designers such as Azzedine Alaia in the early 1980s. [1]
